content: 1. Initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) outside of healthcare facilities must be carefully identified and evaluated to ensure its effectiveness and safety. Research is needed to determine the optimal size and skill set of community treatment teams to support such initiatives. 2. Evidence suggests that ART initiation outside of healthcare facilities may have significant implications for household spending and catastrophic costs, which warrants further investigation. 3. Rapid initiation of ART, including same-day initiation, should be offered to all individuals diagnosed with HIV after confirmation of their diagnosis and clinical assessment. This recommendation is strongly supported by high-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents, though evidence for children is less certain. 4. Rapid ART initiation is defined as starting treatment within seven days of an HIV diagnosis. Priority should be given to individuals with advanced HIV disease for assessment and initiation. 5. Same-day ART initiation should be offered to individuals who are ready to begin treatment. This recommendation is supported by high-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents, but evidence for children remains less certain. 6. The implementation of same-day ART initiation should include strategies to improve treatment uptake, adherence, and retention. These strategies may involve tailored patient education, counseling, and support. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends that nurses be authorized to initiate and maintain ART. However, the adoption of this recommendation in national policies varies across countries. 8. Some studies have reported poorer retention in care when ART is initiated on the same day compared to less rapid initiation, though this is not universally observed. 9. Patient perspectives emphasize the importance of good counseling and respectful, non-judgmental healthcare personnel in supporting ART initiation and adherence. 10. A systematic review identified various strategies to accelerate ART initiation and uptake, including interventions targeting clients, healthcare providers, and the health system. These approaches have been associated with increased ART uptake, viral load suppression at 12 months, and retention in care. 11. For individuals established on ART, clinical visits should be scheduled every 3–6 months, preferably every six months if feasible. ART refills should also last 3–6 months, with six-month refills being ideal if possible. 12. Coordination of clinical consultations with planned medication pick-ups is recommended to reduce the frequency of visits and improve convenience for patients. 13. Strengthening antiretroviral (ARV) drug supply management is essential to ensure the availability of medications and prevent stock-outs, especially in the context of less frequent medication pick-ups. 14. Differentiated service delivery models, including reduced visit frequency and extended ART refills, have been shown to save patient travel costs and reduce the time required to receive ART, while also lowering health system costs. 15. Financial and nutritional support can play a critical role in improving ART adherence and viral suppression, particularly in food-insecure settings. Nutritional support may include counseling, cash transfers, subsidized food costs, or food vouchers. 16. Pregnant and postpartum women face unique challenges to ART adherence, including biological, social, and economic factors. These challenges may be exacerbated by pregnancy-related conditions such as nausea and vomiting. 17. Adolescents and youth face significant barriers to ART adherence, including peer pressure and stigma. Approximately 38% of adolescents globally are suboptimally adherent to ART, with substantial regional variation. 18. Peer counseling, mobile phone text messages, reminder devices, cognitive behavioral therapy, and fixed-dose combination regimens have demonstrated effectiveness in improving ART adherence and viral load suppression. 19. Nutritional assessment, care, and support are essential components of HIV care, as severe food insecurity is associated with suboptimal ART adherence and failure to suppress viral loads. 20. Financial support programs should aim to reduce out-of-pocket costs for people living with HIV, including costs related to drugs, diagnostics, and clinical services, while supporting transportation and decentralizing care. 21. Pregnant women should have the option to choose where to receive ART care, but this must be coordinated with antenatal care to ensure comprehensive and patient-centered services. 22. Addressing stigma, discrimination, and lack of disclosure to partners, family, and the community is critical for improving ART adherence, particularly among vulnerable populations. 23. Service delivery barriers, such as poor-quality clinical practices, gaps in provider knowledge, and limited access to services, must be addressed to improve ART outcomes. 24. Research is needed to evaluate the outcomes of less frequent clinical visits and drug refills, particularly beyond six months, to optimize care for various populations.
